spectrum.definition: how a series' variance is spread over frequencies, from slow swings to fast jitter
spectrum.excludes: the timing or phase of the swings, which the spectrum does not record

spectral-flatness.field: signal processing (speech coding) and the theory of stationary processes
spectral-flatness.definition: the geometric mean of a power spectrum divided by its arithmetic mean; it is 1 for white noise and near 0 when a few frequencies hold most of the variance
spectral-flatness.excludes: flatness of the series itself in time, and measures that use the spectrum's entropy instead of its geometric mean

ks-bound.field: the theory of weakly stationary processes
ks-bound.definition: the smallest one-step error variance any linear predictor can reach on a weakly stationary series, equal to the exponential of the average log spectrum; one minus the flatness is therefore the most variance a linear one-step forecast can remove
ks-bound.excludes: nonlinear predictors on non-Gaussian series, multi-step forecasts, and series whose statistics drift over time

stationary.definition: a series whose mean and autocovariance do not change over time
stationary.excludes: series with trends, level shifts or drifting variance, such as a machine whose load changes between the halves

periodogram.definition: the squared Fourier transform of a series after its ends are faded with a Hann window, used as a raw estimate of the power spectrum at each Fourier frequency
periodogram.excludes: smoothed or averaged spectrum estimates such as Welch's method, which we report only as secondaries

ar-model.definition: a linear forecast of the next value from a weighted sum of the last p values, with the weights fitted by least squares; p is the order
ar-model.excludes: models with moving-average terms, external inputs or nonlinear terms

aic.definition: the Akaike information criterion, a fit score that adds a penalty of two per fitted parameter, used here to choose the autoregressive order
aic.excludes: choice by held-out error, which would use the test half

one-step-skill.definition: one minus the mean squared error of one-step-ahead forecasts on the test half, divided by the test half's variance; 0 matches forecasting the mean and 1 is perfect
one-step-skill.excludes: skill at longer horizons and skill measured on the data used to fit the model

phase-surrogate.definition: a copy of a series with the same power spectrum and random Fourier phases, so it keeps the autocorrelation and is Gaussian and stationary by construction
phase-surrogate.excludes: shuffling in time, which also destroys the spectrum

violation.definition: a series whose excess skill over the bound beats that of at least 38 of its own 39 phase-randomised surrogates, which happens to 5 percent of Gaussian stationary series by chance
violation.excludes: a series whose skill merely exceeds the point bound, which estimation error makes common

spearman.definition: the correlation between the ranks of two quantities across cases; 1 means the same order, 0 no relation of order
spearman.excludes: agreement in size, since two quantities can share an order and differ in scale

analogue.definition: a forecast that finds the k past states most like the present one and averages what came next; it can follow nonlinear structure a linear model misses
analogue.excludes: trained nonlinear models such as neural networks

wilson.definition: a 95 percent interval for a proportion that stays inside 0 and 1 and behaves well when the count is small

bh.definition: a rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05
bh.excludes: corrections that control the chance of any false call at all, such as Bonferroni
